Research Interests: SLA, Digital language learning, Adult learning & SDL, Mobile-learning, Curriculum Design
Title: Contrastive syntax: Prepositions in English and in Arabic
Description: Historically, English and Arabic do not derive from the same language family; English belongs to the Indo-European language family, whereas Arabic is a Semitic language. Consequently, this affects the way foreign language learners learn English, and it is also related to the problems they encounter while using prepositions. McCarthy (1972; cited in Hamdallah & Tushyehh, 1993) states that the English prepositions are troublesome even to some non-native language teachers. English contains some simple and complex prepositions, and Arabic encloses separable and inseparable prepositions. Upon comparing and contrasting the prepositions in both English and Arabic languages, attention should be drawn towards the source of difficulty and the linguistic problems that Arab EFL learners face, the types of common errors they make, and the pedagogical recommendations that might help EFL learners overcome the mentioned difficulties.

Native and Non-native English Language Teachers: A deficit or a difference
H Jaber - 2016
Cited by 2 Related articles
Research Interests: SLA, Digital language learning, Adult learning & SDL, Mobile-learning, Curriculum Design
Title: Native and Non-native English Language Teachers: A deficit or a difference
Description:
The controversy about the effectiveness of the native English-speaking teachers (NESTs) and the non-native English-speaking teachers (non-NESTs) is not a new dichotomy in language teaching and learning. It has been a debatable issue in EFL/ESL research because it bears two opposite points of view and has been a researchable issue by many scholars in EFL and ESL contexts (Medgyes, 1992; Davies, 2003; Cook, 2008). According to Chomsky (1965) The native speaker is: a) the object of linguistic theory, b) the only reliable source of linguistic data, and c) the ‘ideal speaker-listener’.
English has become a means for universal and global communication and is, therefore, described as a ‘lingua franca’(ELF), so countries such as the United States and England are not considered now the only source of standard variety. Many researchers believe that the variety of English that one person speaks plays a role in giving this person an identity (Madiano, 2009; cited in Brown, 2013; p. 7). In most L2 learning contexts, the instructor is considered a “primary source of comprehensible input”, however, others might argue that the huge advance of multimedia is influencing L2 learners to a great extent.

Title: Discourse Analysis Methods
Journal: Unpublished Term Paper for the Degree of PhD in Applied Linguistics. Beirut Arab University
Description: Discourse analysis is a broad field of study that analyzes language in a variety of ways and using different approaches and analytical processes (Wetherell, Taylor, & Yates, 2001a). A discourse is a system of meaning related to a broader socio-cultural context which investigates language in use. It is concerned with whole text and is mainly divided into: 1) Spoken Discourse Analysis, and 2) Written Discourse analysis. It has been argued that Discourse Analysis (DA) is more concerned with naturally occurring data than in made-up language.
